category: Linear Algebra II: Tensors, Structured Matrices & Geometric Transforms
description: Tensor algebra (contraction, products, symmetries), matrix predicates, additional decompositions and matrix functions, structured and special matrices (Toeplitz, Hankel, Hilbert, Fourier, Vandermonde, permutation, block-diagonal), triangularization and minors, and the TransformationFunction family for affine, rotation, scaling and shearing transforms.

tools.name: TensorContract
tools.description: Contracts (sums over) pairs of slots of a tensor, e.g. TensorContract[t, {{1, 2}}] is the trace over slots 1 and 2. Works symbolically on tensors declared with $Assumptions (Element[t, Arrays[{n, n}]]) and numerically on explicit arrays; combined with TensorProduct it expresses arbitrary index contractions without loops.
tools.usage: TensorContract[tensor, {{i1, j1}, {i2, j2}, ...}]

parameters.name: {{i, j}, ...}
parameters.description: Pairs of slot indices to contract.

tools.example:
TensorContract[TensorProduct[a, b], {{2, 3}}] == a.b (* for matrices *)
TensorContract[IdentityMatrix[3], {{1, 2}}] (* 3 *)
(* Frobenius inner product *)
TensorContract[TensorProduct[m, m], {{1, 3}, {2, 4}}]

tools.name: TensorProduct
tools.description: Outer (tensor) product of arrays or symbolic tensors, giving a tensor whose rank is the sum of the ranks; Outer[Times, ...] is the explicit-array equivalent and KroneckerProduct the matrix-flattened version. TensorWedge gives the antisymmetrized (exterior) product used for differential forms and HodgeDual the Hodge dual.
tools.usage:
TensorProduct[t1, t2, ...]
t1 \[TensorProduct] t2
TensorWedge[t1, t2]
HodgeDual[tensor]
HodgeDual[tensor, dim]
tools.example:
TensorProduct[{1, 2}, {3, 4}] (* {{3, 4}, {6, 8}} *)
TensorWedge[{1, 0, 0}, {0, 1, 0}]
HodgeDual[{a, b, c}] (* antisymmetric matrix *)

tools.name: TensorTranspose
tools.description: Permutes the slots of a tensor according to a permutation (list or Cycles), the general form of Transpose with level lists; TensorRank, TensorDimensions and TensorSymmetry return rank, dimensions and symmetry (Symmetric, Antisymmetric, ZeroSymmetric) of explicit or symbolic tensors. Use them in index gymnastics for stress, elasticity and curvature tensors.
tools.usage:
TensorTranspose[tensor, perm]
TensorRank[tensor]
TensorDimensions[tensor]
TensorSymmetry[tensor]

parameters.name: perm
parameters.description: Permutation list such as {2, 3, 1} or Cycles[...].

tools.name: TensorReduce
tools.description: Simplifies symbolic tensor expressions built from TensorProduct, TensorContract, TensorTranspose and Dot using declared symmetries and dimensions ($Assumptions with Element[t, Arrays[dims, Reals, symmetry]]); TensorExpand expands products and sums over tensor operations. They allow index-free symbolic tensor algebra.
tools.usage:
TensorReduce[expr]
TensorReduce[expr, Assumptions -> assum]
TensorExpand[expr]
Element[t, Arrays[{n, n}, Reals, Symmetric[{1, 2}]]]

tools.name: Symmetrize
tools.description: Symmetrizes an array with respect to a symmetry specification (Symmetric, Antisymmetric, or a general Symmetric[{slots}] / permutation-group symmetry), returning either a full array or a compact SymmetrizedArray representation; LeviCivitaTensor[d] gives the totally antisymmetric epsilon tensor. Essential for building elasticity, curvature and Levi-Civita based expressions.
tools.usage:
Symmetrize[array]
Symmetrize[array, Antisymmetric[All]]
Symmetrize[array, Symmetric[{1, 2}]]
SymmetrizedArray[array, sym]
LeviCivitaTensor[d]

parameters.name: sym
parameters.description: Symmetric[slots], Antisymmetric[slots], ZeroSymmetric[slots] or a list of {perm, phase} generators.

tools.name: SymmetricMatrixQ
tools.description: Matrix structure predicates: SymmetricMatrixQ, AntisymmetricMatrixQ, HermitianMatrixQ, AntihermitianMatrixQ, OrthogonalMatrixQ, UnitaryMatrixQ, NormalMatrixQ, DiagonalMatrixQ, SquareMatrixQ, UpperTriangularMatrixQ, LowerTriangularMatrixQ and DiagonalizableMatrixQ. All accept a Tolerance option for approximate matrices and SameTest for symbolic entries; use them to pick algorithms (Cholesky vs LU) and to validate inputs.
tools.usage:
SymmetricMatrixQ[m]
HermitianMatrixQ[m]
OrthogonalMatrixQ[m]
UnitaryMatrixQ[m]
UpperTriangularMatrixQ[m]
DiagonalizableMatrixQ[m]
SymmetricMatrixQ[m, Tolerance -> 10^-8]

parameters.name: Tolerance
parameters.description: Option: allowed deviation for approximate numbers.

tools.example:
SymmetricMatrixQ[{{1, 2}, {2, 1}}] (* True *)
OrthogonalMatrixQ[RotationMatrix[Pi/3]] (* True *)
q = QRDecomposition[RandomReal[1, {4, 4}]][[1]]; UnitaryMatrixQ[q, Tolerance -> 10^-10]

tools.name: PositiveDefiniteMatrixQ
tools.description: Definiteness predicates: PositiveDefiniteMatrixQ, PositiveSemidefiniteMatrixQ, NegativeDefiniteMatrixQ, NegativeSemidefiniteMatrixQ and IndefiniteMatrixQ test the (Hermitian part of the) matrix by attempting a Cholesky factorization or eigenvalue check. Use them before CholeskyDecomposition, in optimization second-order tests, and to validate covariance matrices.
tools.usage:
PositiveDefiniteMatrixQ[m]
PositiveSemidefiniteMatrixQ[m]
NegativeDefiniteMatrixQ[m]
IndefiniteMatrixQ[m]
tools.example:
PositiveDefiniteMatrixQ[{{2, -1}, {-1, 2}}] (* True *)
PositiveDefiniteMatrixQ[{{a, 0}, {0, 1}}] (* stays conditional; use with Assuming[a > 0, ...] *)
hessian = D[f, {{x, y}, 2}] /. sol; PositiveDefiniteMatrixQ[hessian]

tools.name: UpperTriangularize
tools.description: Zeroes the elements below the k-th superdiagonal (UpperTriangularize) or above the k-th subdiagonal (LowerTriangularize), returning the triangular part of a matrix; Band builds banded SparseArrays and Diagonal extracts diagonals. Use them for extracting Cholesky/LU factors, building triangular systems and masking matrices.
tools.usage:
UpperTriangularize[m]
UpperTriangularize[m, k]
LowerTriangularize[m]
LowerTriangularize[m, k]
SparseArray[{Band[{1, 1}] -> 2, Band[{1, 2}] -> -1, Band[{2, 1}] -> -1}, {n, n}]

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Diagonal offset (0 = main diagonal, 1 = strictly upper).

tools.example:
UpperTriangularize[{{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}, {7, 8, 9}}, 1] (* strictly upper part *)
lap = SparseArray[{Band[{1, 1}] -> 2, Band[{1, 2}] -> -1, Band[{2, 1}] -> -1}, {100, 100}];

tools.name: HessenbergDecomposition
tools.description: Gives {p, h} with h upper Hessenberg and p unitary such that m == p.h.ConjugateTranspose[p], the standard preprocessing step of the QR eigenvalue algorithm; BunchKaufmanDecomposition factors symmetric indefinite matrices and is used internally by LinearSolve for such systems. Both complement LU/QR/Cholesky/Schur/Jordan.
tools.usage:
HessenbergDecomposition[m]
BunchKaufmanDecomposition[m]
tools.example:
{p, h} = HessenbergDecomposition[RandomReal[1, {5, 5}]];
Chop[p.h.ConjugateTranspose[p] - m]

tools.name: MatrixLog
tools.description: Principal matrix logarithm, the inverse of MatrixExp (used to recover generators of Lie groups, continuous-time rates from transition matrices and interpolating rotations); MatrixMinimalPolynomial gives the minimal polynomial. Both are exact for symbolic input and numerically stable for machine matrices.
tools.usage:
MatrixLog[m]
MatrixMinimalPolynomial[m, x]

parameters.name: m
parameters.description: Square matrix (no eigenvalues on the negative real axis for the principal log).

tools.example:
MatrixLog[RotationMatrix[Pi/4]] (* generator {{0, -Pi/4}, {Pi/4, 0}} *)
MatrixExp[MatrixLog[m]] == m // Chop
MatrixMinimalPolynomial[{{2, 0}, {0, 2}}, x] (* -2 + x *)

tools.name: Minors
tools.description: Minors[m] gives the matrix of (n-1)x(n-1) minors and Minors[m, k] all k x k minors (optionally applying a function instead of Det); Adjugate gives the adjugate (classical adjoint) so that m.Adjugate[m] == Det[m] IdentityMatrix; Permanent computes the matrix permanent. Used in cofactor expansions, Cramer's rule and combinatorial counting.
tools.usage:
Minors[m]
Minors[m, k]
Minors[m, k, f]
Adjugate[m]
Permanent[m]

tools.name: DrazinInverse
tools.description: The Drazin generalized inverse of a square matrix (agreeing with the ordinary inverse for nonsingular matrices), used for singular linear systems, Markov chain analysis and differential-algebraic equations; PseudoInverse is the Moore-Penrose inverse for rectangular least-squares problems.
tools.usage: DrazinInverse[m]

tools.name: LinearSolveFunction
tools.description: The object returned by LinearSolve[m] (no right-hand side): it stores the factorization of m and solves m.x == b for any b by applying it as a function, so repeated solves with the same matrix cost only a triangular substitution. Also produced for SparseArray matrices (with iterative or direct Method) - the idiomatic way to solve many systems with one matrix.
tools.usage:
ls = LinearSolve[m]
ls[b]
ls[bmatrix]
LinearSolve[m, Method -> "Cholesky"]
LinearSolve[sparse, Method -> "Krylov"]

parameters.name: m
parameters.description: Square (or rectangular) matrix, dense or sparse.

tools.example:
ls = LinearSolve[SparseArray[{Band[{1, 1}] -> 4, Band[{1, 2}] -> -1, Band[{2, 1}] -> -1}, {1000, 1000}]];
sols = ls /@ Table[RandomReal[1, 1000], {50}]; (* 50 solves, one factorization *)

tools.name: ToeplitzMatrix
tools.description: Constructs a Toeplitz matrix (constant along diagonals) from its first column and row, HankelMatrix a Hankel matrix (constant along anti-diagonals) and HilbertMatrix the classic ill-conditioned Hilbert matrix. These arise in convolution, autocorrelation (Levinson), system identification and conditioning tests.
tools.usage:
ToeplitzMatrix[n]
ToeplitzMatrix[{c1, c2, ..., cn}]
ToeplitzMatrix[col, row]
HankelMatrix[n]
HankelMatrix[col, row]
HilbertMatrix[n]
HilbertMatrix[{m, n}]
tools.example:
ToeplitzMatrix[{1, 2, 3}, {1, 4, 5}] (* {{1, 4, 5}, {2, 1, 4}, {3, 2, 1}} *)
(* convolution as a Toeplitz matrix product *)
T = ToeplitzMatrix[PadRight[h, n], PadRight[{First[h]}, n]]
LinearSolve[HilbertMatrix[12], ConstantArray[1, 12]] (* exact rationals *)

tools.name: FourierMatrix
tools.description: The n x n unitary DFT matrix (so that Fourier[v] == FourierMatrix[n].v up to convention), with FourierDCTMatrix and FourierDSTMatrix for cosine/sine transforms and HadamardMatrix for Walsh-Hadamard. Use them to express transforms as explicit linear operators, e.g. in compressed sensing or to derive circulant diagonalizations.
tools.usage:
FourierMatrix[n]
FourierMatrix[n, FourierParameters -> {a, b}]
FourierDCTMatrix[n]
FourierDCTMatrix[n, k]
FourierDSTMatrix[n]
HadamardMatrix[n]

tools.name: VandermondeMatrix
tools.description: Vandermonde matrix with rows {1, x, x^2, ...} for given nodes (rectangular n x k form available), the matrix of polynomial interpolation and least-squares polynomial fitting; CauchyMatrix gives 1/(x_i - y_j). Represented as a structured array so Det, LinearSolve and Inverse use specialised fast algorithms.
tools.usage:
VandermondeMatrix[{x1, x2, ..., xn}]
VandermondeMatrix[{x1, ..., xn}, k]
CauchyMatrix[{x1, ...}, {y1, ...}]

tools.name: PermutationMatrix
tools.description: Structured-array representation of a permutation matrix from a permutation list (or Cycles), with O(n) storage and fast Det, Inverse, Dot and LinearSolve; BlockDiagonalMatrix, BlockUpperTriangularMatrix, BlockLowerTriangularMatrix, UpperTriangularMatrix, LowerTriangularMatrix, JordanMatrix and CompanionMatrix are the other structured constructors (13.1+). Normal converts any of them to an ordinary array.
tools.usage:
PermutationMatrix[permlist]
BlockDiagonalMatrix[{m1, m2, ...}]
UpperTriangularMatrix[m]
LowerTriangularMatrix[m]
CompanionMatrix[poly, x]
JordanMatrix[{{lambda1, k1}, {lambda2, k2}}]
Normal[structured]
tools.example:
P = PermutationMatrix[{3, 1, 2}];
Normal[P]
P.{a, b, c} (* {c, a, b} *)
Normal[BlockDiagonalMatrix[{{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}, {{5}}}]]
CompanionMatrix[x^3 - 2 x + 1, x] // Normal

tools.name: RotationMatrix
tools.description: Explicit rotation matrices: RotationMatrix[theta] in 2D, RotationMatrix[theta, {x, y, z}] about an axis in 3D, RotationMatrix[{u, v}] rotating u onto v, and RotationMatrix[theta, {u, v}] in the plane spanned by u and v (any dimension); EulerMatrix builds rotations from Euler angles and EulerAngles extracts them. ScalingMatrix, ShearingMatrix and ReflectionMatrix give the other linear maps.
tools.usage:
RotationMatrix[theta]
RotationMatrix[theta, {x, y, z}]
RotationMatrix[{u, v}]
EulerMatrix[{alpha, beta, gamma}]
EulerMatrix[{alpha, beta, gamma}, {a, b, c}]
EulerAngles[r]
ScalingMatrix[{sx, sy}]
ShearingMatrix[theta, {1, 0}, {0, 1}]
ReflectionMatrix[v]
tools.example:
RotationMatrix[Pi/2, {0, 0, 1}].{1, 0, 0} (* {0, 1, 0} *)
RotationMatrix[{{1, 0, 0}, {0, 1, 0}}]
EulerAngles[RotationMatrix[0.3, {1, 1, 1}]]

tools.name: TransformationFunction
tools.description: The object representing a geometric transformation (returned by RotationTransform, TranslationTransform, ScalingTransform, ShearingTransform, ReflectionTransform, RescalingTransform, AffineTransform and FindGeometricTransform); apply it to points or lists of points, compose with Composition or Dot, invert with InverseFunction, and extract the homogeneous matrix with TransformationMatrix. It is the argument of GeometricTransformation, TransformedRegion and ImageTransformation.
tools.usage:
tf = RotationTransform[theta, center]
tf[{x, y}]
tf /@ points
TransformationMatrix[tf]
InverseFunction[tf]
Composition[tf1, tf2]
AffineTransform[{m, v}]
TranslationTransform[v]
ScalingTransform[{sx, sy}]
ScalingTransform[{sx, sy}, center]
ReflectionTransform[v]
RescalingTransform[{{xmin, xmax}, {ymin, ymax}}, {{umin, umax}, {vmin, vmax}}]
tools.example:
tf = Composition[TranslationTransform[{1, 0}], RotationTransform[Pi/2]];
tf[{1, 0}] (* {1, 1} *)
TransformationMatrix[tf] (* 3x3 homogeneous matrix *)
Graphics[{GeometricTransformation[Rectangle[], ShearingTransform[Pi/6, {1, 0}, {0, 1}]]}]
TransformedRegion[Disk[], ScalingTransform[{2, 1}]]

tools.name: TransformationMatrix
tools.description: Gives the homogeneous (n+1)x(n+1) matrix of a TransformationFunction, and AffineTransform / TransformationFunction[m] build a transformation from a matrix - the bridge between the symbolic transform objects and explicit matrices for OpenGL-style pipelines, robotics (homogeneous coordinates) and image warping.
tools.usage:
TransformationMatrix[tf]
TransformationFunction[mhomogeneous]
AffineTransform[m]
AffineTransform[{m, v}]
tools.example:
m = TransformationMatrix[RotationTransform[Pi/3, {0, 0, 1}].TranslationTransform[{1, 2, 3}]];
TransformationFunction[m][{0, 0, 0}]

tools.name: DesignMatrix
tools.description: Builds the design matrix of a linear model (rows of basis functions evaluated at the data points, with an intercept column by default) exactly as LinearModelFit does; useful for custom regression (ridge, weighted, constrained) with LeastSquares or LinearSolve, and for inspecting collinearity.
tools.usage:
DesignMatrix[data, {f1, f2, ...}, x]
DesignMatrix[data, {f1, ...}, {x, y}, IncludeConstantBasis -> False]

tools.name: CoefficientArrays
tools.description: Extracts the arrays of coefficients of a polynomial system as SparseArrays {c0, c1, c2, ...} so that the system equals c0 + c1.vars + c2.vars.vars + ...; the standard way to turn linear equations into matrix form (m, b) for LinearSolve, or quadratic forms into matrices for QuadraticOptimization.
tools.usage:
CoefficientArrays[polys, vars]
CoefficientArrays[eqns, vars]
{b, m} = CoefficientArrays[eqns, vars]

parameters.name: polys / eqns
parameters.description: List of polynomials or equations (lhs - rhs is used).

tools.name: GaussianMatrix
tools.description: Kernel and shape matrices: GaussianMatrix[r] (normalised Gaussian kernel of radius r, with derivative variants), BoxMatrix, DiskMatrix, DiamondMatrix and CrossMatrix (structuring elements of 0s and 1s). Used for convolution (ListConvolve, ImageConvolve) and morphological operations.
tools.usage:
GaussianMatrix[r]
GaussianMatrix[{r, sigma}]
GaussianMatrix[r, {n1, n2}]
BoxMatrix[r]
DiskMatrix[r]
DiamondMatrix[r]
CrossMatrix[r]

parameters.name: r
parameters.description: Radius (matrix is (2r+1) square); {rx, ry} for rectangular.

tools.example:
ListConvolve[GaussianMatrix[2], data, {3, -3}]
Dilation[img, DiskMatrix[3]]
GaussianMatrix[1, {1, 0}] (* x-derivative of Gaussian kernel *)

tools.name: CenterArray
tools.description: Places an array at the centre of a larger array of zeros (or a given background) of specified dimensions, e.g. to embed a kernel into a full-size array for FFT-based convolution or to zero-pad symmetrically. Complements ArrayPad and PadLeft/PadRight.
tools.usage:
CenterArray[array, n]
CenterArray[array, {n1, n2, ...}]
CenterArray[array, dims, x]
tools.example:
CenterArray[{{1, 1}, {1, 1}}, {4, 4}]
kernelFull = CenterArray[GaussianMatrix[3], Dimensions[image]];

tools.name: RangeSpace
tools.description: RangeSpace[m] gives a minimal list of vectors spanning the range (column space) of a matrix, the counterpart of NullSpace for the image; introduced in Version 14.3. In earlier versions obtain a column-space basis with Orthogonalize of the columns or by deleting zero rows from RowReduce[Transpose[m]]; MatrixRank gives its dimension (use the Tolerance option or SingularValueDecomposition thresholds for numerical matrices).
tools.usage:
RangeSpace[m]
Orthogonalize[Transpose[m]] (* pre-14.3 alternative *)
DeleteCases[RowReduce[Transpose[m]], {0 ..}]
NullSpace[m]
MatrixRank[m, Tolerance -> 10^-10]
tools.example:
m = {{1, 2, 3}, {2, 4, 6}, {1, 0, 1}};
RangeSpace[m] (* two basis vectors, 14.3+ *)
MatrixRank[m] (* 2 *)
NullSpace[m] (* {{-1, -1, 1}} *)
tools.notes: RangeSpace requires Version 14.3 or later; the catalog's reference version is 14.2, so prefer the Orthogonalize/RowReduce idioms for portable code.

tools.name: Arnoldi
tools.description: Method setting of Eigenvalues/Eigenvectors/Eigensystem for large sparse matrices: Eigenvalues[m, k, Method -> {"Arnoldi", "Criteria" -> "RealPart", "Shift" -> sigma}] computes only k eigenvalues near a shift (Lanczos for symmetric), avoiding dense O(n^3) work. Also "FEAST" for interval eigenvalues of Hermitian problems, and the Cutoff/Tolerance options for numerical rank decisions.
tools.usage:
Eigenvalues[sparse, k]
Eigenvalues[sparse, -k] (* smallest *)
Eigenvalues[sparse, k, Method -> {"Arnoldi", "Shift" -> 0, "Criteria" -> "Magnitude"}]
Eigenvalues[herm, Method -> {"FEAST", "Interval" -> {a, b}}]

parameters.name: k
parameters.description: Number of eigenvalues (negative for the smallest).

tools.example:
lap = SparseArray[{Band[{1, 1}] -> 2, Band[{1, 2}] -> -1, Band[{2, 1}] -> -1}, {5000, 5000}];
Eigenvalues[lap, -5, Method -> {"Arnoldi", "Shift" -> 0}] (* 5 smallest *)

tools.name: Band
tools.description: Band[{i, j}] -> v inside SparseArray fills the diagonal band starting at position {i, j} (Band[{i, j}, {imax, jmax}] limits it, and a list value cycles along the band), the fastest way to build tridiagonal, banded and block-banded sparse matrices. Related sparse idioms: pattern rules {i_, j_} /; cond -> v, inspection with s["NonzeroPositions"], s["NonzeroValues"], s["Density"], and LinearSolve with Method -> "Multifrontal" or "Krylov".
tools.usage:
SparseArray[{Band[{1, 1}] -> 2, Band[{1, 2}] -> -1, Band[{2, 1}] -> -1}, {n, n}]
SparseArray[{Band[{1, 1}] -> {a, b, c}}, {3, 3}]
SparseArray[{Band[{1, 1}, {n, n}, {1, 2}] -> 1}, {n, 2 n}]
s["NonzeroPositions"]
s["Density"]
